body: Leverage taken on in an upcycle was the common thread in every big Indian sector wipeout. Infrastructure and EPC in 2007–12 (Lanco, GVK, Punj Lloyd, Gammon) used debt plus aggressive bids. Thermal IPPs in 2010–13 had untied PPAs and imported coal. Steel in 2011–16 (Bhushan, Essar, Monnet) ended in IBC. Real estate in 2008–19 (Unitech, Jaypee) diverted customer advances. NBFCs in 2018–19 (IL&FS, DHFL) borrowed short to lend long. Private banks in 2018–20 (Yes Bank) grew loans ahead of deposits. Retail in 2019–20 (Future Group) expanded on debt. The survivors and compounders entered the downturn with net cash or low leverage and gained share when weak players exited: UltraTech and Shree in cement, JSW after its 2016 recovery, HDFC Bank and Kotak in 2008 and 2018, Bajaj Finance after 2008, Radico through FY17–21 deleveraging (D/E 0.77 to 0.15). Sector-specific balance-sheet tests: lenders on deposit/CASA franchise and ALM; cyclicals on net debt/EBITDA under 2x at mid-cycle margins; EPC on working capital and receivables over a year; developers on net debt against annual collections; utilities on discom receivables. Lesson: in cyclical and financial sectors, screen out stretched balance sheets first, then pick on growth.

data.lesson: Survive first: screen leverage and funding structure before growth; downturn share gains build the next decade's winners.

title: Across Indian sectors, the downcycle balance sheet decides the long-term winner

body: Bertrand, Mehta and Mullainathan, 'Ferreting Out Tunneling: An Application to Indian Business Groups' (Quarterly Journal of Economics 117(1), 2002; ~1,730 S2 citations), Indian firms 1989-1999 from CMIE Prowess. Tunnelling, moving resources from firms where the promoter has low cash-flow rights to firms where they have high rights, is illegal and hard to observe, so they measured it by how firms respond to industry earnings shocks. Group firms where the controlling family has low ownership respond significantly less to positive shocks to their own industry, and firms where the family has high ownership respond to shocks hitting OTHER group firms. Money leaks out of the low-ownership affiliates, and the effect is economically significant and concentrated in non-operating profit lines. Khanna and Palepu, 'Is Group Affiliation Profitable in Emerging Markets?' (Journal of Finance 55(2), 2000; ~2,700 citations), 1993 data on about 1,300 firms: affiliates of the most diversified groups outperformed unaffiliated firms (Tobin's q and ROA), because groups substituted for missing capital, labour and managerial markets in pre-reform India. Moderately diversified groups underperformed. Replicated: both are canonical; later work (Siegel-Choudhury 2012; Gopalan-Nanda-Seru 2007 on intra-group loans) confirms tunnelling and internal capital markets in India. Use for us: check the promoter's economic stake in the listed company versus private entities. A listed company where the promoter owns less, and which trades heavily with promoter private firms (royalties, ICDs, purchases, guarantees), is where value leaks. Link to the related-party tests and the 'cash cow funds the sick sibling' record.

data.bmm_method: sensitivity to own vs other-group industry shocks

title: Indian business groups: tunnelling is measurable (Bertrand-Mehta-Mullainathan 2002), yet affiliation with the most diversified groups added value in the 1990s (Khanna-Palepu 2000)

body: Pre-registered in research_notes/Backtests/india_annual_report_text.md s0 before sampling. Frame = 2,021 NSE symbols with an announcement Jun-Sep 2023 (survivorship-free for mid-2023 listings), seed 2026112203; 810 walked -> 350 eligible (200 text firms + 150 control-only). 585 ARs (5.1 GB, median 6.9 MB) downloaded via new `nse_fetch.py annual_reports`, pdftotext'd, PDFs deleted; section parser usable for 77% (MD&A) / 83% (auditor+CARO) of pairs; BRSR pages excluded by construction. Go rule (wins. mean <= -5%, median < 0, t <= -1.5; H3: >=10 flags, wins <= -10%) failed on all three. Calibration: all text-firm events -4.0/-6.6% vs controls (sample noise), so read relative: changers +1.9 pp (MD&A) / +5.8 pp (auditor) vs all events. Lottery profile as US (medians -17%/-10%, hit 37-42%). Secondary only: stalest auditor text (Q5) -15.2% (t -2.54) but P1 -28.5% / P2 -2.0% -> hypothesis, not finding. Auditor-change cases: 'trouble' items (restatement, qualification, regulatory/tax action, default) median -10% but mean +3%; technical EoMs (schemes, mergers, policy changes) carry no signal. Use: judgment cue in stage-4 deep dives (diff auditor report + CARO vs prior year), not a rule.

auditor_cases_12m_excess.item: EoM OCPS from scheme not converted
